issues.legal_issue: A decomposed recovered body may be identified through witness testimony and distinctive physical features, and the condition of the body does not by itself defeat proof of the victim’s death and identity.
material_facts: The recovered body was decomposed, with some soft tissue eaten away, but the scalp hair remained intact.
A village watchman who had known the deceased since childhood identified the body by its facial features, thick moustache, grey hair patch, and a coin tied at the waist.
The informant and another witness also identified the body as that of the deceased.
The medical and investigative evidence did not establish that identifying features were wholly absent.
issues.conclusion: The courts below were entitled to find that the recovered body was that of the deceased; the challenge based on the body’s condition failed.
issues.legal_principle: Proof of the corpus delicti is not an indispensable legal requirement where strong evidence establishes death and the accused’s responsibility; discovery of a body is a rule of caution, not law. Identification and proof depend on the evidence and circumstances of the case. The Court relied on Rama Nand v. State of Himachal Pradesh, Ram Gulam Chaudhary v. State of Bihar, and Lakshmi v. State of U.P.; the charge considered was under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code.

predicates.decomposed_body_recovered: A body was recovered in a decomposed condition.
predicates.distinctive_features_remained: The recovered body retained physical features capable of assisting identification.
predicates.witnesses_familiar_with_victim_identifie: Witnesses who knew the victim identified the recovered body as the victim.

issues.definition: When a criminal conviction is appealed, a decomposed recovered body does not defeat identification if distinctive features remained or familiar witnesses identified it.

issues.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to examine every available or independent witness does not by itself undermine a case supported by truthful, reliable evidence.
material_facts: The prosecution did not examine some witnesses named in the charge sheet.
The prosecutor stated that some witnesses were inimically disposed towards the informant, and the defence produced no material to disprove that explanation.
Several eyewitnesses testified, their accounts were more or less consistent, and the defence did not point to anything discrediting their testimony.
The Court considered that independent witnesses may be reluctant to testify in village disputes involving land.
issues.conclusion: The non-examination of the other witnesses did not warrant an adverse inference or undermine the prosecution case on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution is not invariably required to examine every available witness; the quality and intrinsic worth of the evidence matter more than its quantity. Witnesses essential to unfolding the prosecution narrative should be called, and omission may matter where it causes prejudice or leaves an essential account unexplained. The Court relied on Sheelam Ramesh v. State of A.P., Pohlu v. State of Haryana, Balram Singh v. State of Punjab, State of U.P. v. Anil Singh, Habeeb Mohammad v. State of Hyderabad, and Sahaj Ram v. State of U.P.

predicates.omitted_witnesses_not_shown_to_be_essent: The omitted witnesses were not shown to be essential to the prosecution narrative or their omission to have prejudiced the accused.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal, non-examination alone does not undermine the prosecution case when the examined witnesses are reliable and the omitted witnesses are not shown to be essential or their omission prejudicial.

issues.legal_issue: An approximate medical estimate of the time of death does not require rejection of the prosecution account when the body’s condition makes precise timing difficult and the estimate’s basis is unexplained.
material_facts: The post-mortem evidence gave an approximate interval of about ten days before examination for the death.
The body had been submerged for more than five days, was decomposed, lacked rigor mortis, and had soft tissue eaten away by fish.
The autopsy surgeon did not explain the basis for the estimate and could not pinpoint the exact time of death.
issues.conclusion: The approximate medical estimate did not justify disbelieving the prosecution case.
issues.legal_principle: Medical evidence may not enable a doctor to state the exact time of death, particularly where decomposition and other conditions complicate estimation; an unexplained approximate estimate should not be treated as precise. The Court relied on Ramreddy Rajeshkhanna Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh and referred to Modi’s Medical Jurisprudence.

issues.legal_issue: Common intention may be inferred in a group assault even when the prosecution cannot attribute a specific overt act to each participant.
material_facts: The accused arrived and acted as a group, forcibly taking two people onto a boat.
The group assaulted one of them with weapons, causing his death.
The eyewitness who escaped could not realistically pinpoint each participant’s individual act during the group attack.
The medical evidence was consistent with injuries inflicted by sharp weapons, and the accused had arrived armed.
issues.conclusion: The circumstances attracted common-intention liability despite the absence of proof of each accused’s individual overt act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code applies where the participants’ conduct establishes a shared common intention; a specific overt act by each participant is not necessary. The Court relied on Bishna alias Bhiswadeb Mahato v. State of West Bengal.

issues.legal_issue: A written account and later eyewitness testimony do not materially contradict each other when the written account reasonably bears the interpretation given by the courts.
material_facts: The written report stated that the accused arrived and forcibly took the informant and deceased toward the water on a boat.
The defence argued that the report implied the accused arrived on foot and boarded a boat already waiting at the water.
The High Court read the report as describing the accused arriving by boat and taking the two men aboard, consistent with the witnesses’ testimony.
issues.conclusion: The written report and the eyewitness testimony contained no material inconsistency on how the accused arrived and took the victims.
issues.legal_principle: The alleged inconsistency must be assessed by reading the written account as a whole and comparing its reasonable meaning with the testimony; a strained interpretation does not establish a contradiction.

predicates.written_account_reasonably_supports_same: The written account, read reasonably, describes an event sequence consistent with the later testimony.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal, an alleged inconsistency is not material when the written account reasonably supports the same event sequence as the testimony.
